newsitem.title: USA: Calif. city hopes to keep 'supergiant' field alive.
newsitem.headline: Calif. city hopes to keep 'supergiant' field alive.

text.p: As oil production dries up in California, geologists in this economically troubled city are hoping to nearly double current reserves by probing deeper into its once-rich petroleum fields.

With oil prices higher and more accurate seismic data in their arsenal, geologists in Long Beach are willing to gamble that the city's premier field, Wilmington, can still provide the city with much-needed revenue.
The "supergiant" Wilmington field, the third most prolific producing in U.S. history, still holds about 6.4 billion barrels, or most of the city's reserves, by current estimates.

But even after 65 years of production, some geologists believe that hidden, deep pockets of oil can be tapped, pushing reserves in the field to as high as 12 billion barrels, and adding about 10 years to the field's current estimated lifespan.
"There's still a lot of oil in the ground here," James Hempill, a manager in the Long Beach Department of Oil Properties, told Reuters.
At its peak in 1969, some 245,000 barrels a day were flowing from the field, but in recent years output has been reduced to nearly a trickle of 54,000 barrels a day.

Tapping new wells could come within six to eight months, if the city and the field's operator, Atlantic Richfield Co, extend a development well it began drilling last week. That well, which should hit in one of Wilmington's prolific offshore segments, is about 10,000 feet deep.
But hidden riches could lie just beyond that, at 13,000 feet, according to City of Long Beach geologist Ron Clarke.

Clarke reckons seismic activity has pushed oil-bearing rock into areas not yet touched by the bit. One of those formations, known as a "sub thrust play," lies at the 13,000-foot-level and could contain 100 million barrels.
Long Beach geologists discovered the possibility of a play using technology that helped Wyoming producers find oil in similar kinds of rocks
What's more, the deeper oil is under more pressure and therefore is heated longer and cooked into higher quality light oil -- a sharp contrast to most California crudes which are on the heavy side.

But the risks for failure, hitting "a dry hole," are high. Wells in known producing fields are dry about 12 out of 13 tries, city geologists say. And at the cost of betweeen $1 and $2 million per well, efforts to revive the city-owned wells in the Wilmington field present a risk to taxpayers.
"It's public money we're drilling with...so do we have a right to gamble with it?" Clarke said.

But current prices, around $15 a barrel for Wilmington type grades, are high compared to when they dipped to below $10 a barrel in early 1994. Stronger prices are indeed making the risks more economic and, if the risk pays off, Clarke say similar finds in the region could open up large new reserves.
"It opens up a whole slew up places and maybe a whole new set of plays in the Los Angeles basin," Clarke said.
